title: Editorial & Review Board
kicker: The named people who write, review and sign off ProudTek articles
summary: This page lists every person authorised to author or co-sign editorial content on proudtek.com. The board exists so every byline on the site resolves to a real human with verifiable experience, and so every technical article is co-signed by a reviewer who has direct working experience with the standard or product family the article discusses. The list below is the current roster as of the modifiedAt date; historical contributors are preserved in the log at /about/corrections/ so that older articles carrying their byline remain attributable. Reader challenges to a reviewer's credentials are welcome and are handled under the same process as correction requests.
heroPoints: Every editorial article on proudtek.com is signed by a person listed on this page.
Technical articles (anything citing a standard, a chip family, or a regulatory requirement) must be co-signed by a named reviewer on the roster.
Reviewers are required to disclose any equity or paid relationship with a vendor they review; disclosures are published on each reviewer's entry below.
Before any reviewer is added to the board, identity and at least one external credential are verified by the editor-in-chief.

sections.title: Editor-in-Chief
sections.intro: Responsible for final sign-off on every editorial article. Sets the editorial calendar, approves corrections, and recruits the review board.

features.title: Peter Zhang — Founder & Editor-in-Chief
features.text: Founder of ProudTek with 18 years in RFID/NFC manufacturing; operates the in-house RFID laboratory in Shenzhen. Final editorial sign-off on guides, comparisons and compatibility articles. Focus areas: custom NFC business-card manufacturing, hotel-lock RFID compatibility, RFID laundry-tag selection for hospitality, and UHF RAIN deployments.

callout.text: For correction requests, reviewer nominations, or editorial partnerships, contact editors@proudtek.com. Enquiries are triaged within 2 business days.

callout.label: Why we publish empty slots
callout.text: Publishing the reviewer roster with visible TODOs is more honest than populating it with made-up names. An article that would require a reviewer in a TODO slot is either (a) held for publication until the slot is filled, (b) co-signed by the editor-in-chief plus a named external reviewer whose credential is cited in the article's sources block, or (c) published under the institutional Editorial Board byline with a note that technical review on that topic is handled jointly until a permanent reviewer is in place.

sections.title: How reviewers are vetted
sections.intro: The board is not self-nominated. Before anyone is added, identity and at least one external credential are verified.

items.label: 1 — Nomination
items.text: A reviewer is nominated by an existing board member or applies directly via editors@proudtek.com. Applications include a CV and at least one link to a public professional profile.

items.label: 2 — Identity check
items.text: The editor-in-chief confirms identity by a documented interview (video, recorded) and by cross-checking at least one public profile (LinkedIn, ORCID, company About page, patent filing, conference talk, standards-body roster).

items.label: 3 — Credential verification
items.text: At least one verifiable credential is checked against the issuing authority: university degree, engineering registration, standards-body member directory, or patent register. Unverifiable credentials are either dropped from the public bio or flagged as 'self-reported'.

items.label: 4 — Scope & disclosure
items.text: Reviewer signs the disclosure form listing equity and paid relationships with any vendor they might cover. Disclosures are published on the reviewer's entry.

items.label: 5 — Trial period
items.text: First three reviews are also checked by the editor-in-chief before publication. A reviewer whose trial reviews reveal an accuracy issue is not added to the public roster.

sections.title: Removing a reviewer
sections.intro: We keep the list honest by retiring reviewers who no longer meet the criteria.
bullets: Reviewers inactive for 12 months are moved to an 'emeritus' list; articles they previously signed keep their byline.

A reviewer whose disclosure changes materially (e.g. takes a paid role at a vendor they reviewed) is asked to update their disclosure; if that creates an unmanageable conflict, they are removed from the roster and the affected articles are re-reviewed.

A reviewer whose public record turns out to include a credential that cannot be verified is removed immediately; the editor-in-chief reviews every article that carried their signature and logs any corrections.

faq.question: Why are some reviewer slots listed as TODO?
faq.answer: Because we would rather publish the roster with empty slots than fabricate reviewer entries. When an article on a topic in an empty slot is ready to publish, it is either held until we recruit a reviewer with verifiable credentials, co-signed by the editor-in-chief plus a named external reviewer (whose credential is cited in the article's sources block), or shipped under the institutional Editorial Board byline until a permanent reviewer is in place.

faq.question: How do I apply to the review board?
faq.answer: Send a CV, a link to at least one public professional profile, and a one-paragraph note on your specialty area to editors@proudtek.com. We respond within 2 weeks, either with a trial brief or with a note explaining why we cannot onboard at this time.

faq.question: Can I challenge a reviewer's credentials?
faq.answer: Yes. Send the URL of the reviewer's profile and the specific credential you believe is incorrect to editors@proudtek.com. We treat challenges to a reviewer's credentials with the same process as factual corrections. We acknowledge within 2 business days and either update the entry or publish a justification within 5 business days.

faq.question: Is external paid reviewing influenced by sales?
faq.answer: No. Reviewers are paid per review assignment at a fixed rate that does not depend on the article's conclusion, the product it recommends, or subsequent sales. The contract explicitly names the editor-in-chief as the single point of editorial escalation; no sales team member can direct a reviewer's conclusion.
